ns0:entry.ns0:title: [TED]Here’s your reminder that you are enough — and you always will be #WorldMentalHealthDay

ns2:group.ns2:title: Here’s your reminder that you are enough — and you always will be #WorldMentalHealthDay
ns2:group.ns2:description: On paper, Blake Mycoskie is a glowing success story: he founded TOMS Shoes, building a global brand that has given away more than 100 million pairs of shoes to children in need. Yet despite his success, his struggle with depression nearly cost him his life. In this personal talk, he explores the all-too-common shame that keeps people suffering in silence — and shares his new mission to spread the simple yet powerful message that each of us is inherently enough. (Note: This talk includes discussion of suicide and depression.) (Recorded at TED2026 on April 17, 2026)

ns2:group.ns2:title: These are the inherent human skills that machines can’t replace #TEDTalks
ns2:group.ns2:description: As AI reshapes work, school and love, what part of being human can't a machine take over? In a wide-ranging conversation, psychotherapist Esther Perel and TED's vision steward Sal Khan provide their unique takes on the answer. From personalized learning and AI companions to "emotional capitalism" and the rituals we create to live with uncertainty, the two explore if we're getting better at living or just getting better at optimizing. (This conversation is part of “TED Intersections,” a series featuring thought-provoking conversations between experts navigating the ideas shaping our world.)

ns0:entry.ns0:title: [TED]How to Clean Up the World’s Dirtiest Industry | Joojin Kim | TED

ns2:group.ns2:title: How to Clean Up the World’s Dirtiest Industry | Joojin Kim | TED
ns2:group.ns2:description:
Climate strategist Joojin Kim spent years convincing banks across South Korea to stop funding coal, and it worked. Now he's aiming that same playbook at a new target: maritime shipping, a hidden engine of the global economy — and one of the world's dirtiest industries. He breaks down how the whole system converges in one place and why redirecting finance could transform it into a driver of a clean economy worldwide. (This ambitious idea is part of The Audacious Project, TED's initiative to inspire and fund global change.) (Recorded at TED2026 on April 15, 2026)

ns2:group.ns2:title: Sometimes common ground starts with what both sides can’t afford to lose. #TEDTalks
ns2:group.ns2:description: What if the path to peace starts with self-interest? After four decades inside some of the world's most dangerous conflict zones, mediator Hiba Qasas has learned that most peacebuilding efforts get it wrong from the start. She makes a provocative case that conciliation shouldn't begin with empathy — and reveals how leading with shared incentives brought hundreds of Israeli and Palestinian leaders into active collaboration, even in the midst of war.

ns2:group.ns2:title: Life, like music, was never made to run in straight lines #TEDTalks
ns2:group.ns2:description: Grammy-winning musician Jacob Collier has a name for the feeling that moves through a great piece of music: the wiggle. Watch him break down the idea into its three parts — melody, rhythm and harmony — with nothing but his own voice, a grand piano and Louis Armstrong’s “What a Wonderful World.” Turns out life, like music, was never made to run in straight lines.

ns0:entry.ns0:title: [TED]Good news: Even moving as little as 1 minute every 60 minutes can have health benefits #TEDTalks

ns2:group.ns2:title: Good news: Even moving as little as 1 minute every 60 minutes can have health benefits #TEDTalks
ns2:group.ns2:description: Can a five-minute walk change how you feel all day? Exercise scientist Keith Diaz shows how your body is built for the kind of movement that modern life has quietly erased — and suggests something refreshingly doable: making time for small doses of movement sprinkled throughout the day, as a way to boost your brain and body.

ns0:entry.ns0:title: [TED]The Gravity-Defying Future of Manufacturing | Schendy Kernizan | TED

ns2:group.ns2:title: The Gravity-Defying Future of Manufacturing | Schendy Kernizan | TED
ns2:group.ns2:description:
3D printing promised to reinvent how we make things, but it's mostly stuck producing prototypes with a high level of waste. Designer and TED Fellow Schendy Kernizan found a different way — by printing objects directly into a tub of gel. He explains how this technique eliminates the constraints of gravity, pushing the limits of how we can manufacture objects across medicine, fashion, space travel and more. (Recorded at TED Fellows Films 2026 on April 14, 2026)
